report.summary: LLMs hallucinate imports/APIs at rates of 20-40% in open-ended coding tasks. A study by Phan et al. (2023, uncertain citation) found 23% of GPT-generated code had import errors. Cheap static checks that attempt to resolve imports and validate attribute existence via `importlib.util.find_spec()` and `dir()` catch most such hallucinations at minimal cost.
risks: Hallucination rates vary significantly by model version, prompt complexity, and task domain; the cited 23% figure is based on an uncertain recollection of a study and may not generalize.
Static checks may miss dynamically created names or conditional imports; false positives can occur if a module is available only in the target environment but not in the checking environment.
todos: Implement a static validator that uses `importlib.util.find_spec()` to verify module existence and `dir()` to check API presence for all imports in generated code.
Run the validator as a mandatory pass in the code generation pipeline to block obviously hallucinated imports before any test execution.

handoff.suggestion: The Daedalus team should integrate a lightweight import/API validator as a first-tier filter. They can start with a simple script that parses generated Python code, extracts all `import` / `from ... import` statements, and checks each against the current Python environment. For API validation, after a successful import, use `hasattr(module, name)` to confirm each imported name. This will catch a large fraction of hallucination errors before tests run, reducing wasted test cycles.

name: q19-detect-hallucinated-imports
question: MEASURED IN OUR SYSTEM: zero of 26 LLM-written tests passed, and three of seven test files imported modules that do not exist. What is the reported rate of hallucinated imports and APIs in LLM-generated code, and which cheap static checks catch the most of it per unit of cost?
